source_read: PDF of the NIST author manuscript, AM pp. 1–19 (all pages; Tables 1 and 3 checked on rendered AM pp. 16 and 19; supplementary tables not available). The PDF is filed as PDFs/Cannabis/Sisco_2023_XylazineTestStrips.pdf although it is this paper.

claims.overstatement: None. Two conditions worth stating: the limits are for pure standards in water with all ten strips clearly positive (no test band), and acetonitrile above about 10% v/v made these benzodiazepine strips read negative, so the negatives at the high end of the etizolam range may be partly solvent-related; the negative at 0.01 mg/mL, where the other benzodiazepines read positive, is not.
claims.note: The authors attribute the etizolam result possibly to a 'thiazole ring'; etizolam has a thiophene ring (a thienodiazepine, as they also say). That the strip is the same product as Laing et al.'s is not stated; only the maker (BTNX) is.

claims.overstatement: None. The editors' comparison (250 ng/mL for the expired strips is not worse in absolute terms than 500 ng/mL for the in-date ones) is arithmetically right, but the two are different products (listed cut-offs 0.02 and 0.2 µg/mL) and no in-date strip of the expired product was tested, so neither the editors' comparison nor the authors' 'loss in sensitivity' isolates the effect of age.
claims.note: 'One lot each' is inferred from Table 1 (one expiry date per strip type), not stated. The abstract's 'little to no change in sensitivity' for expired strips sits beside a fentanyl limit 12.5 times the listed cut-off and a methamphetamine limit 5 times that of in-date strips.

key_findings.correction: Minor source inconsistency: the text gives 2:3 acetonitrile:water as the mixture without band development (AM p. 5); the Figure 2 caption names 1:1 and 3:2 (AM p. 15).
Per Table 3, fentanyl and its analogues reacted with none of the seven strip types, so the parenthetical restriction to four strip types is unnecessary.

The note's 'in-date fentanyl strips of another lot' undersells the difference: their listed cut-off is 0.2 µg/mL against 0.02 for the expired strips, so they are probably a different product or version (the paper does not say). The editors' comparison itself is right (0.25 < 0.5 µg/mL).
28.75 µg in 1 mL = 11.5 times the 2.5 µg/mL limit, 'roughly ten times' as stated.

reporting_issues.note: The † mark is defined in Table 3's notes and used in no cell (rendered AM p. 19).
My count on the rendered AM p. 17: 9 + 11 + 2 + 11 = 33 'a' marks, against 'thirty' in the text (AM p. 3).

risk_of_bias.note: Overall high: agree. Instrument: disagree. The study compares strip readings with the known concentrations of prepared solutions, which METHODS §5.3 (0.3.1) files as test-accuracy with QUADAS-2, as was done for sc_bergh_2021, the same kind of study. My own QUADAS-2 judgments, for an adjudicator deciding on re-appraisal. (1) Sample selection: HIGH. Pure reference standards at chosen concentrations; a known-positive / known-negative panel of 79 chosen by the authors, not exhaustive (5 benzodiazepines, 3 nitazenes); acetonitrile added to 33 stocks, 2 stocks cloudy suspensions. Applicability concern high: no street samples or mixtures (authors' limitation, AM p. 11). (2) Index test: HIGH. Visual reading by laboratory staff who knew analyte and concentration; number of readers and blinding not reported; photographs not used for blinded re-reading. The positivity rule (no test band) and the limit rule (all strips clearly positive) were pre-specified, but the faint-negative calls near threshold are subjective. Applicability concern: trained laboratory readers. (3) Reference standard: LOW. Known content by gravimetric or volumetric preparation from four commercial suppliers, not verified analytically. Unclear for the 33 acetonitrile-assisted and 2 suspension stocks, whose effective concentration in the strip solution is uncertain. (4) Flow and timing: UNCLEAR. Every analyte was tested at both concentrations, but replicates differ by sub-study (10 strips per limit level, 2 per cross-reactivity cell, 3 in the heat and expiry studies). The fentanyl strip had no 10-strip limit study, only heat-study triplicates. Solvent-affected benzodiazepine results were explained rather than repeated without acetonitrile. Expired strips were compared with labels or other products, not same-lot fresh strips. The full results are in supplementary tables not read. Overall QUADAS-2: HIGH, with high applicability concerns for drug checking in practice.

interpretation_gap.note: Minor, at the upper end. The Conclusions twice contradict the results: heat ('unaffected', AM p. 10, against a tenfold loss for xylazine strips) and expiry ('little to no change', AM p. 1, against fivefold for methamphetamine and 12.5 times the label for fentanyl). 'Generally work for identification of drug products' (AM p. 11) describes something not tested. An adjudicator may consider 'substantial'.

missed: Design: under METHODS §5.3 (0.3.1) this is a test-accuracy study against known concentrations; re-file it and appraise with QUADAS-2 (my domain judgments in risk_of_bias.note), as for sc_bergh_2021.

The fentanyl strip's 0.5 µg/mL limit comes only from the heat sub-study's triplicates: the 10-strip limit study excluded fentanyl (AM p. 6). So it is less robust than the other limits, which analysis.effect_sizes lists it beside without comment.

The authors attribute etizolam's non-reaction possibly to a 'thiazole ring' (AM p. 7). Etizolam has a thiophene ring (a thienotriazolodiazepine, as they also say), so the structural explanation is misstated; the etizolam result itself stands.
